title: Presentation Skills: Speak with Confidence
tagline: Calm your nerves, build a clear talk and deliver it well, then master slides, tough questions, online meetings and high-stakes pitches.
takeaways: Build a talk around one message
Use voice and body with purpose
description:
Most people feel nervous before they present. That is normal, and it does not have to stop you. Presenting is a skill, not a gift, and you can learn it step by step. This quest is only about presenting: to a class, to your team, to a client or on a video call.

**Basic stages (free):**

- **Nerves and preparation:** calm your body, understand your audience, find one key message and practise the smart way.
- **Structure:** a strong opening, three clear points and a close with a call to action.
- **Voice and body:** pace, pauses, eye contact, gestures, and how to present standing or sitting.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**

- **Slides and stories:** one idea per slide, visuals over text, simple charts and stories that make data stick.
- **The hot seat:** answering questions, handling tough audiences, cutting a talk to fit the time and recovering from mistakes.
- **Online and high stakes:** video calls, pitches to clients and management, panels and interview presentations, plus a practice-and-feedback plan.

Follow Maryam, a final-year student in Lahore, and her friends as they turn shaky first attempts into talks that win marks, jobs and clients. All people and businesses in this course are fictional.
audience: Students who present in class, at seminars or for a final-year project
Fresh graduates and job seekers facing presentation tasks in interviews
Office staff who give updates to their team or management
Sales staff and small-business owners who pitch to clients
Anyone who feels nervous speaking in front of people, in a room or online
outcomes: Manage nerves with simple breathing, preparation and practice routines
Analyse an audience and build a talk around one clear key message
Structure a talk with a strong opening, three points and a clear call to action
Use pace, pauses, eye contact, gestures and posture to sound and look confident
Design clear slides, simple charts and short stories that make the message stick
Handle questions, tough audiences, time cuts and mistakes calmly
Present well on video calls and in pitches, panels and interviews, and keep improving with feedback

Their mentor Imran, a training manager in Islamabad, helps all three, from the first nervous practice to the biggest room. Clear each stage and find your steady voice.

sessions.title: Beating Nerves and Preparing: Audience, One Key Message and Practice
sessions.summary: Learn why nerves happen and how to calm them, then prepare the smart way: understand your audience, choose one key message and practise out loud in rounds. Your win: a one-sentence message and a practice plan for your next talk.
objectives: Explain what nerves do to the body and use two simple ways to calm them
Ask five questions to understand any audience before you plan
Turn a broad topic into one clear key message in a single sentence
Practise out loud in short rounds instead of memorising a script

cards.title: Three weeks to go
cards.setting: A university canteen in Lahore, late afternoon, chai on the table.

lines.text: Welcome to the Steady Voice Quest. Your first stop is a busy university canteen in Lahore, where a student is staring at her laptop.
My final-year project presentation is in three weeks. Just thinking about it, my hands go cold. Last time my voice shook so much I forgot my second slide.
Same here, yaar. I have to pitch to my first client in Karachi soon. I keep thinking everyone will notice I am nervous.
Can I tell you a secret? Almost every speaker feels nervous. The ones who look calm have simply learned what to do with that energy.
So what do I do? Write the whole thing and learn it by heart?
No. We start with three things: who is listening, the one message you want them to remember, and how you will practise. Nerves get smaller when preparation gets bigger.

scenes.heading: Nerves are energy
scenes.narration: A faster heartbeat, a dry mouth and shaky hands are your body getting ready for something important. They feel bad, but they are not dangerous, and listeners often notice much less of them than you feel.

scenes.heading: Know your audience
scenes.narration: Before you write anything, think about the people listening. What do they already know, what do they need, and what will they do after your talk?

scenes.heading: Find one key message
scenes.narration: Decide the single idea you want people to remember. If they forget everything else, this one sentence should stay with them.

scenes.heading: Practise out loud
scenes.narration: Reading your notes in your head is not practice. Say the talk out loud, in short rounds, and it starts to feel familiar.

scenes.heading: Calm the body
scenes.narration: On the day, arrive early, breathe slowly with a longer breath out, and focus on helping the audience rather than on yourself.

cards.title: The preparation path
cards.caption: Prepare in this order. Slides come last, not first.

items.label: Audience
items.detail: Who is listening, what they know and what they need from you.

items.label: Purpose
items.detail: What you want them to know, feel or do by the end.

items.label: One key message
items.detail: One sentence that sums up your whole talk.

items.label: Outline
items.detail: Three main points that support the message.

items.label: Practise aloud
items.detail: Short rounds out loud, improving each time.

items.label: Final check
items.detail: Time, room or link, equipment and a backup plan.

cards.question: Maryam wants to start preparing by opening the slide software and making a title slide. What should she do first?
options: Choose a colourful slide theme so she feels motivated
Write out every word of the talk and learn it by heart
Think about her audience and what they need from the talk
Search online for the most impressive opening line she can find
cards.explanation: Good preparation starts with the audience and purpose. Once she knows who is listening and what they need, her message, outline and slides become much easier to plan.

cards.title: Why nerves happen and what helps
cards.body:
When you face something important, your body releases stress hormones. Your heart beats faster, your breathing gets quick and shallow, and your hands may shake. This is a normal alarm, not a sign that you are bad at speaking.

Three things help most:

- **Slow breathing:** breathe in gently through your nose and breathe out slowly, a little longer than the breath in. This tells your body it is safe.
- **Preparation:** the more familiar your talk feels, the less your mind panics.
- **A helpful focus:** think 'How can I help these people?' instead of 'What will they think of me?'

You do not need to remove nerves completely. A little energy keeps you alert and makes you sound alive.

cards.back: Students, managers, clients, parents? Their role shapes the words and examples you choose.
Do not explain basics to experts, and do not use jargon with beginners. Pitch it at their level.
A decision, an update, a new skill or a reason to buy? Build your talk around that need.
Cost, time, risk or change? Answer worries before they become questions.
Approve, sign up, try something, give marks? Know the action you want.
Respect their time. A clear ten-minute talk beats a rushed twenty-minute one.

cards.title: A topic versus a key message
cards.caption: A topic is what you talk about. A key message is what you want people to remember.

items.label: Final-year project
items.left: My project on a library booking app
items.right: Our app cuts the wait for study rooms, and it is ready to test

items.label: Sales pitch
items.left: Our company's water filters
items.right: This filter gives your office safe water without buying bottles

items.label: Team update
items.left: Last month's deliveries
items.right: Deliveries are faster, but two routes still need fixing

items.label: Catering offer
items.left: My catering menu
items.right: Fresh, home-style lunches, delivered on time, every school day

cards.title: Twenty-five slides, ten minutes
cards.situation: Usman's manager asks him to present the new water filter range to the sales team in Karachi on Monday. He has ten minutes. He has copied 25 slides of product specifications from the company brochure and plans to go through them all quickly so nothing is missed.

choices.text: Ask what the team needs most, choose one key message and keep only the details that support it.
choices.outcome: Usman learns the team mostly needs to know which filter suits which customer. He builds a clear talk around that, and the team asks good questions. His manager is impressed.

choices.text: Keep all 25 slides but speak faster so he finishes in ten minutes.
choices.outcome: He finishes, but nobody remembers much. Speaking faster to fit more in usually means the audience takes in less.

choices.text: Cut the slides to 12 by removing every second slide.
choices.outcome: The talk is shorter, but it is cut by number, not by importance. Some key points are lost and some details remain.

cards.title: Practise in rounds
cards.prompt: Put these practice steps in a sensible order, from first try to final run.
steps: Talk through your outline out loud, using only short notes
Time yourself and see which parts are too long
Fix the opening and the close so they sound smooth
Record a run on your phone and watch it back once
Do a full practice in front of a friend and ask for one improvement
Do a final run in a setting close to the real one

cards.question: Which of these is the best one-sentence key message for Nadia's talk to a school committee?
options: Catering
Everything you might want to know about my catering business
Fresh, home-style lunches, delivered on time every school day
My history, my kitchen, my menu, my prices and my team
cards.explanation: A key message is a single, clear idea the audience can remember and act on. 'Catering' is just a topic, and the other two are lists that try to say everything.

cards.title: Nadia finds her message
cards.body:
Nadia has been invited to speak for five minutes to the parents' committee of a private school in Faisalabad. Her first plan has eight parts: her story, her kitchen, every dish, prices, staff and more.

Imran asks her: 'What do these parents worry about most?' Nadia thinks. 'That their children eat healthy food that arrives on time.'

So her key message becomes: **'Fresh, home-style lunches, delivered on time, every school day.'**

Now every part of her talk has a job. Her kitchen photos prove 'fresh'. A sample menu proves 'home-style'. Her delivery plan proves 'on time'. The full price list goes into a handout instead.

cards.title: A two-minute calm-down routine
cards.body:
Try this just before you speak:

1. Stand or sit tall, feet flat on the floor.
2. Breathe in gently for a count of four.
3. Breathe out slowly for a count of six. Repeat four or five times.
4. Relax your shoulders and unclench your jaw.
5. Say your first sentence quietly to yourself.

Keep water nearby for a dry mouth. Avoid trying something new on the day, such as a new outfit or a new way of speaking.

cards.title: Helpful or unhelpful preparation?
cards.prompt: Sort each habit by how it affects your preparation.

items.text: Practising out loud several times in short rounds
Learning a full script word for word
Checking the room, projector or video link early
Making slides before deciding your message
Writing your key message in one sentence
Staying up all night to add more slides
Planning what you want the audience to do after
Reading your notes silently and calling it practice

cards.title: Take-aways from the Waiting Room
items: Nerves are normal body energy; slow breathing and preparation calm them.
Start with the audience: who they are, what they know and what they need.
Choose one key message you can say in a single sentence.
Build three supporting points before you make any slides.
Practise out loud in short rounds instead of memorising a script.

cards.prompt: Think of your next presentation, at university, at work or for your business. Who will be listening, and what is your one key message in a single sentence?

quiz.question: What is a 'key message' in a presentation?
options: The title written on your first slide
The one idea you most want the audience to remember
A list of every topic you will cover
A full list of every topic and detail you plan to cover in the talk
quiz.explanation: A key message is the single main idea of your talk. Everything else in the talk should support it.

quiz.question: Which is a normal sign of nerves before speaking?
options: Losing the ability to read
Forgetting your own name for a week
Feeling no energy at all
A faster heartbeat and a dry mouth
quiz.explanation: A faster heartbeat, quick breathing, a dry mouth and shaky hands are common signs of the body's normal stress response.

quiz.question: Which breathing pattern helps most to calm nerves just before a talk?
options: Breathing out slowly, a little longer than the breath in
Taking many fast, short breaths through the mouth to wake yourself up
Holding your breath for as long as you can
Breathing only from the top of the chest
quiz.explanation: A slow breath out that is longer than the breath in helps the body relax. Fast, shallow breathing makes nerves feel worse.

quiz.question: In what order should you prepare a talk?
options: Audience, purpose, key message, outline, practice
Slides, script, practice, audience, message
Practice, slides, audience, outline, message
Title, slides, animations, notes, audience
quiz.explanation: Start with the audience and purpose, then the key message and outline, then practise. Slides support the plan; they do not create it.

quiz.question: Usman's audience are senior engineers who already know the product well. What should he avoid?
options: Spending a long time explaining basics they already know
Using a clear structure with three points and a short summary at the end
Asking what decision they need to make
Keeping to the time he was given
quiz.explanation: Knowing the audience's level means not wasting experts' time on basics. Clear structure, focus on their needs and good timing still matter.

quiz.question: Why is memorising a full script word for word risky?
options: It always makes the talk too short
Audiences are not allowed to see scripts, so it breaks the rules of most venues
It stops you from using any slides
One forgotten word can make you lose your place and freeze
quiz.explanation: A memorised script is fragile. If you lose one line, it is hard to recover. Knowing your points and practising them in your own words is safer.

quiz.question: Which question helps you most to find your key message?
options: How many slides can I fit into the time?
What one thing should they remember?
Which font will look the most professional?
How can I show everything I know about the topic?
quiz.explanation: Asking what one thing the audience should remember forces you to choose the main idea instead of trying to say everything.

quiz.question: Which focus usually helps a nervous speaker most?
options: Thinking about what people will think of them
Watching for anyone who looks bored
Thinking about how to help the audience
Trying to sound exactly like a famous speaker
quiz.explanation: Shifting attention from yourself to the audience's needs reduces self-consciousness and gives your talk a clear purpose.

quiz.question: Maryam practises by reading her notes silently three times. What is the best advice?
options: Read the notes silently three more times
Skip practice so she sounds natural and fresh on the day of the talk
Practise out loud, in short rounds, and time herself
Practise only the thank-you slide
quiz.explanation: Silent reading does not prepare your voice, timing or flow. Speaking out loud in rounds builds real familiarity.

quiz.question: Nadia's talk has eight parts. Her key message is about fresh, on-time school lunches. What should she do with her full price list?
options: Move it to a handout and keep the talk on her key message
Read every price aloud so nothing is missed
Put it on the first slide in small text
Leave it out completely and refuse to discuss prices with anyone who asks
quiz.explanation: Details that do not support the key message can go in a handout. That keeps the talk focused while still giving people the information.

sessions.title: Structuring a Talk: Strong Opening, Three Points and a Clear Close
sessions.summary: Give your talk a shape people can follow: an opening that grabs attention, three main points with clear signposts, and a close that sums up and asks for action. Your win: a full outline for a five-minute talk.
objectives: Choose a strong opening instead of a weak or apologetic one
Organise the body of a talk into three clear main points
Use signposts so the audience always knows where they are
Close with a short summary and a specific call to action

cards.title: The opening nobody heard
cards.setting: A small office in Karachi's Shahrah-e-Faisal area, Monday morning.

lines.text: Usman is practising a five-minute update for his manager about a new delivery route plan.
'Assalam o alaikum. My name is Usman. Sorry, I am not very good at this. Today I will talk about some things about the routes.'
Stop there. In ten seconds you apologised and said 'some things'. What do you want your manager to know?
That if we change two routes, drivers finish an hour earlier. But I thought I should explain everything first.
Then say that first. Open with the result, give three reasons, and finish by asking for what you need. People follow a clear shape.
So: 'Two route changes can get our drivers home an hour earlier. Here is how, and here is what I need from you.' That sounds much stronger.

cards.title: The shape of a clear talk

scenes.heading: Hook
scenes.narration: Start with something that makes people want to listen: a question, a short story, a problem or a striking fact from your own work.

scenes.heading: Map
scenes.narration: Tell them what is coming in one line, for example 'I will cover three things: the problem, the plan and the cost.'

scenes.heading: Three points
scenes.narration: Most talks work well with three main points. It is enough to feel complete and few enough to remember.

scenes.heading: Signposts
scenes.narration: Short phrases like 'My second point is...' or 'So what does this mean?' help people follow you.

scenes.heading: Summary
scenes.narration: Repeat your key message and the three points briefly, so the main idea sticks.

scenes.heading: Call to action
scenes.narration: End by telling people exactly what to do next: approve, sign up, try, reply or decide.

cards.title: The talk skeleton
cards.caption: A simple frame that works for a class, a team, a client or a video call.

items.label: Opening hook
items.detail: Grab attention in the first few sentences.

items.label: Key message and map
items.detail: Say your main idea and what is coming.

items.label: Point one
items.detail: First supporting idea, with an example.

items.label: Point two
items.detail: Second supporting idea, with an example.

items.label: Point three
items.detail: Third supporting idea, with an example.

items.label: Summary and call to action
items.detail: Repeat the message and ask for a clear next step.

cards.question: Which opening line is strongest for Usman's route update?
options: Sorry, I am not very good at presentations, so please bear with me
Today I will talk about some things about the routes
First let me tell you the full history of our delivery department
Two small route changes can get our drivers home an hour earlier
cards.explanation: A strong opening leads with something the audience cares about. Apologies, vague phrases and long history make people switch off before the point arrives.

cards.title: Five ways to open
cards.body:
The first minute decides whether people lean in or check their phones. Try one of these:

- **A question:** 'How many of you have waited twenty minutes for a free study room?'
- **A short story:** 'Last Tuesday, a driver called me at 9 pm, still on the road.'
- **A problem:** 'Our customers love the product, but half our calls are complaints about delivery.'
- **A striking fact you can check:** use your own data, for example from your class survey or team records. Never make one up.
- **A picture or object:** hold up the item or show one strong photo.

Avoid opening with an apology, a long list of thank-yous or 'Today I will talk about...'. Thank the host briefly, then hook.

cards.title: Match the opening to its type
cards.prompt: Match each opening line to the type of hook it uses.

pairs.left: 'Have you ever missed a lecture because the bus was late?'
pairs.right: A question that connects to the audience's life

pairs.left: 'Last week, a customer in Clifton called us three times.'
pairs.right: A short, real-feeling story

pairs.left: 'In our class survey, most of us said we skip breakfast.'
pairs.right: A fact from your own data

pairs.left: 'We sell a great product, but deliveries keep arriving late.'
pairs.right: A problem the audience cares about

pairs.left: Holding up a lunch box and opening it
pairs.right: An object that makes the idea visible

cards.title: Weak close versus strong close
cards.caption: The last thing you say is often what people remember.

items.label: Last words
items.left: 'So yes, that's it, I think. Any questions?'
items.right: 'Two route changes, one hour saved. Can we test them next week?'

items.label: Summary
items.left: No summary, the talk just stops
items.right: Key message and three points repeated in two sentences

items.label: Action
items.left: Nothing for the audience to do
items.right: One clear, specific next step

items.label: Energy
items.left: Voice fades and eyes drop to the floor
items.right: Steady voice, eye contact, a short pause before 'Thank you'

cards.title: Results without a point
cards.situation: Maryam's final-year project talk starts with ten minutes on her research method, then shows a table of test results, then ends with 'That's all, thank you.' Her supervisor says the examiners will not know why the project matters. She has two days to fix the structure.

choices.text: Open with the problem her app solves, give three points (what she built, how it was tested, what it showed) and close with what should happen next.
choices.outcome: The examiners understand the value in the first minute. The method and results now support a clear message, and the close asks for feedback on the next version.

choices.text: Keep the same order but add a slide called 'Conclusion' at the end.
choices.outcome: A conclusion slide helps a little, but the audience still waits ten minutes to learn why the work matters.

choices.text: Add more detail to the method section so it looks more serious.
choices.outcome: The talk gets longer and the point gets harder to find. More detail does not fix a missing structure.

cards.title: Build Nadia's five-minute talk
cards.prompt: Put the parts of Nadia's talk to the school parents in a clear order.
steps: Open with a question: 'What did your child eat for lunch yesterday?'
State her key message: fresh, home-style lunches, on time, every school day
Point one: how the food is cooked fresh each morning
Point two: a sample week of balanced menus
Point three: how deliveries reach the school on time
Summarise and ask parents to try a free tasting day next Friday

cards.question: What is the main job of a 'signpost' in a talk?
options: To add extra points at the last minute
To fill silence while you think of what to say
To repeat the same slide twice for emphasis
To show the audience where they are in the talk
cards.explanation: Signposts such as 'My second point is...' or 'Now let us look at cost' act like road signs, helping listeners follow the structure.

cards.title: Maryam's new outline
cards.body:
Here is Maryam's final-year project talk after the fix:

- **Hook:** 'Last semester, I waited forty minutes for a study room that was empty all along.'
- **Key message:** 'Our booking app shows which rooms are free in real time, and it is ready for a trial.'
- **Point one:** what the app does, with one screen shown live.
- **Point two:** how it was tested with a group of classmates over two weeks.
- **Point three:** what the tests showed and what still needs work.
- **Close:** 'Free rooms, shown in real time. We would like to run a trial in the library next term. May we have your feedback on that plan?'

The content is the same as before. The shape is what changed.

cards.title: Signpost phrases to borrow
cards.body:
Keep a few of these ready:

- 'I will cover three things today...'
- 'Let us start with the problem.'
- 'My second point is about cost.'
- 'So what does this mean for us?'
- 'Finally...'
- 'To sum up...'
- 'Here is what I am asking for.'

Use 'finally' only once, and only when you really are near the end.

cards.title: Opening, body or close?
cards.prompt: Sort each line into the part of the talk where it fits best.

items.text: 'How many of you have waited for a study room?'
'I will cover three things: the problem, the app and the results.'
'My second point is how we tested the app.'
'Here is one example from the testing week.'
'To sum up: free rooms, shown in real time.'
'Can we start a trial next term?'

cards.title: Take-aways from the Blueprint Desk
items: Open with a hook, not an apology or 'Today I will talk about...'.
Say your key message early and give a one-line map of what is coming.
Organise the body into three main points, each with an example.
Use signposts so the audience always knows where you are.
Close with a short summary and one clear, specific call to action.

cards.prompt: Write the first and last sentence of your next talk. Does the first one make people want to listen, and does the last one tell them exactly what to do?

quiz.question: Why do many talks use three main points?
options: Rules say every talk must have exactly three points, no more and no fewer
Three is enough to feel complete and few enough to remember
Audiences cannot hear more than three sentences
It makes the talk last exactly ten minutes
quiz.explanation: Three points is a practical guide: it gives a sense of completeness without overloading the audience. It is a habit, not a strict rule.

quiz.question: Which of these is a weak way to open a talk?
options: 'Have you ever missed a class because of a late bus?'
'Sorry, I am not good at this, so please be patient.'
'Last week, a customer called us three times.'
'Two small route changes can save each of our drivers about an hour a day.'
quiz.explanation: Apologising at the start lowers expectations and adds nothing. Questions, short stories and clear results are stronger hooks.

quiz.question: What is a 'call to action'?
options: A phone call made during the presentation
The first question from the audience
A slide at the end listing the speaker's phone number and email address
A clear request telling the audience what to do next
quiz.explanation: A call to action asks the audience to take a specific next step, such as approving, trying or signing up.

quiz.question: Usman wants to use a 'striking fact' as a hook. What is the safest source?
options: A number he remembers hearing somewhere
A guess that sounds impressive
His own team's records that he can check and show
A figure he rounds up a little so it sounds bigger and more impressive
quiz.explanation: Facts must be true and checkable. Using your own data, or a reliable source you can name, protects your credibility.

quiz.question: What does a one-line 'map' after the opening do?
options: Tells the audience what is coming so they can follow
Shows a picture of the venue
Lists every slide number in the talk
Replaces the need for a key message, because the map already lists the points
quiz.explanation: A short map, such as 'I will cover the problem, the plan and the cost', prepares listeners and makes the structure easy to follow.

quiz.question: Which closing line is strongest?
options: 'So yeah, that's basically it, I guess.'
'Any questions? No? Okay, thank you.'
'I could say much more about our menu, but sadly we are out of time.'
'Fresh lunches, on time. Will you book a tasting day?'
quiz.explanation: A strong close repeats the key message and asks for one specific action. Fading out or apologising weakens the ending.

quiz.question: Maryam's talk spends ten minutes on method before saying why the project matters. What is the main problem?
options: The method section is too short
She did not use enough slides
The audience waits too long to learn the point
She thanked the examiners too briefly at the start and end of the talk
quiz.explanation: When the purpose comes late, the audience does not know why the details matter. Leading with the problem and message fixes this.

quiz.question: How should each of your three main points be supported?
options: With a longer list of more points
With a joke, whatever the topic
With a new key message for each point, so the talk covers more ground
With an example, a short story or a piece of evidence
quiz.explanation: Points become clear and memorable when backed by an example or evidence. Each point should support the one key message.

quiz.question: Which phrase is a signpost?
options: 'My second point is about delivery times.'
'Um, so, like, okay.'
'I hope this slide is not too small.'
'Can everyone at the back hear me?'
quiz.explanation: A signpost tells listeners where they are in the structure. Filler words and sound checks do not guide the audience through content.

quiz.question: Nadia's talk ends with a summary and 'Thank you'. What is missing?
options: A specific next step for the parents to take
A list of all her ingredients
A second opening hook
An apology for taking up so much of the parents' busy time
quiz.explanation: Without a call to action, the audience may agree but do nothing. Nadia should ask them to do one clear thing, such as book a tasting day.

sessions.title: Voice and Body Language: Pace, Pauses, Eye Contact and Gestures
sessions.summary: Learn to use your voice and body so people trust and follow you: a steady pace, purposeful pauses, warm eye contact, open gestures and a calm stance, whether you stand at the front or sit at a table. Your win: a recorded practice run with one clear improvement.
objectives: Control pace and use pauses instead of filler words
Vary volume and tone so your voice sounds alive and clear
Use eye contact and open gestures to connect with the audience
Present with a confident posture, both standing and sitting

cards.title: The video does not lie
cards.setting: Nadia's kitchen in Faisalabad, evening. Her phone leans against a jar of lentils.

lines.text: Imran bhai, I recorded my practice. I spoke so fast! And I said 'basically' eleven times. I counted.
Recording yourself takes courage. What else did you notice?
I looked at my notes most of the time, and I kept swaying from side to side like a pendulum.
These are the most common habits. The good news is that each one has a simple fix: slow down, pause instead of filling, look up, and plant your feet.
But if I pause, will they not think I forgot?
A pause feels long to you and natural to them. It shows confidence and gives them time to think. Let us practise one.

scenes.heading: Pace
scenes.narration: Nerves make most people speak too fast. Slow down a little, especially for key points, numbers and names.

scenes.heading: Pauses
scenes.narration: A short silence before or after an important line makes it stand out. Pauses also replace filler words like 'um' and 'basically'.

scenes.heading: Volume and variety
scenes.narration: Speak so the back row can hear. Change your tone and speed now and then so your voice does not sound flat.

scenes.heading: Eye contact
scenes.narration: Look at one person for one thought, then move to another part of the room. People feel spoken to, not spoken at.

scenes.heading: Gestures
scenes.narration: Let your hands move naturally to show size, steps or comparisons. Keep them visible, between your waist and shoulders.

scenes.heading: Stance
scenes.narration: Stand with feet about hip-width apart and weight even. Move with purpose, then stop. Sitting? Sit tall, near the front of the chair.

cards.title: Energy and control
cards.caption: Aim for the top right: plenty of energy, used with control.

items.label: Restless
items.detail: Lots of energy but little control: fast speech, pacing, hands fidgeting.

items.label: Engaging
items.detail: Energy with control: varied voice, purposeful pauses, steady stance.

items.label: Hidden
items.detail: Low energy and low control: quiet voice, eyes down, hiding behind notes.

items.label: Steady but flat
items.detail: Calm and controlled but low energy: correct, yet easy to tune out.

cards.question: Nadia says 'basically' many times while she thinks. What is the best replacement?
options: A different filler word, such as 'actually'
A short, silent pause
Speaking faster so there is no time for fillers
A small laugh between sentences
cards.explanation: Filler words fill silence while the brain catches up. A brief pause does the same job and sounds more confident.

cards.title: Eye contact that feels natural
cards.body:
Eye contact helps people trust you. It also lets you see whether they understand.

- **One person, one thought:** look at someone while you finish a sentence, then move to another person in a different part of the room.
- **Include everyone:** sweep left, centre and right, front and back, so no group feels left out.
- **Be respectful:** in many settings in Pakistan, a warm, steady look is fine, but a hard stare can feel rude. Keep it friendly and brief.
- **Notes are for glancing:** look down, find your point, look up, then speak.
- **Large rooms:** if you cannot see faces clearly, look towards small groups, which still feels personal.

cards.title: Nervous habits and what to do instead

cards.back: Pick three key lines to say slowly, and add a pause mark before each one in your notes.
Pause silently instead. Practise by recording yourself and counting fillers each round.
Plant both feet. If you move, walk to a new spot, stop, then speak.

cards.front: Hands in pockets or locked together
cards.back: Rest them loosely at your sides or hold a pen or clicker, and let them move when you explain.
Know your points. Glance at the slide, turn back to the audience, then speak.

cards.front: Voice fading at the end of sentences
cards.back: Breathe before each sentence and keep your volume up to the last word.

cards.title: Standing versus sitting
cards.caption: Both can look confident. Adjust a few habits to suit the setting.

items.label: When
items.left: Class talks, seminars, events and larger rooms
items.right: Meetings, small panels, interviews and video calls

items.label: Posture
items.left: Feet hip-width apart, weight even, shoulders relaxed
items.right: Sit tall near the front of the chair, both feet on the floor

items.label: Gestures
items.left: Bigger, so the back of the room can see them
items.right: Smaller, above the table, so they stay visible

items.label: Movement
items.left: Move with purpose between points, then stand still
items.right: Lean in slightly to show interest; avoid spinning the chair

cards.title: The fixed podium
cards.situation: Maryam's seminar room has a heavy wooden podium with a fixed microphone. When she practises behind it, only her head shows, and she grips the sides tightly. The microphone cannot be moved, and she is the third of eight speakers.

choices.text: Stay near the microphone so she can be heard, but stand slightly to the side, relax her grip and look up often.
choices.outcome: She is heard clearly and more of her body shows. With her hands free, she gestures naturally, and the room feels more connected.

choices.text: Leave the podium and walk around the room without the microphone.
choices.outcome: She feels freer, but people at the back cannot hear her, and the speakers after her are unsure what to do.

choices.text: Stay fully behind the podium and read from her notes to be safe.
choices.outcome: She is heard, but she looks hidden and the audience loses interest. It is safe, but not strong.

cards.title: Match the voice tool to its effect
cards.prompt: Match each way of using your voice to what it does for the audience.

pairs.left: Pause before a key line
pairs.right: Builds attention so the line stands out

pairs.left: Slow down for numbers
pairs.right: Gives people time to take in details

pairs.left: Raise your volume a little
pairs.right: Helps the back row hear and shows energy

pairs.left: Lower your volume for a moment
pairs.right: Draws people in for something important

pairs.left: Change your tone between points
pairs.right: Keeps your voice from sounding flat

cards.question: Usman presents sitting at a meeting table. What should he do with his hands?
options: Keep them under the table so they do not distract
Hold his phone in both hands the whole time
Cross his arms to look serious
Keep them visible above the table and let them gesture naturally
cards.explanation: When sitting, gestures should stay above the table where people can see them. Hidden or crossed arms can make you look closed or nervous.

cards.title: Usman marks his notes
cards.body:
Usman tends to rush. Before his next team update, he prints his outline and marks it:

- a **/** where he will pause
- a word in **bold** that he will say slowly
- a small **↑** where his voice should lift with energy

His opening now reads: 'Two route changes / can get our drivers home / **one hour** earlier.' He practises three times with his phone recording. In the first round he counts fourteen fillers. In the third round, he counts four. He does not need zero; he needs fewer than last time.

cards.title: A quick voice warm-up
cards.body:
Five minutes before you speak, try this somewhere quiet:

1. Hum gently for a few breaths to warm your voice.
2. Say 'ma-me-mi-mo-mu' slowly, then faster, opening your mouth wide.
3. Read your first two sentences aloud at a slower pace than feels natural.
4. Smile and roll your shoulders back.

Drink plain water. Very cold drinks or a lot of tea right before speaking can leave some people with a dry throat.

cards.title: Practise with your phone
cards.prompt: Put these steps for a recorded practice in a useful order.
steps: Set the phone at about eye level, a little way in front of you
Record a full run of your talk without stopping
Watch once with the sound off to check body language
Listen once without watching to check pace, pauses and fillers
Choose one habit to improve in the next round
Record again and compare the two runs

cards.title: Take-aways from the Echo Hall
items: Slow down for key lines, numbers and names; nerves usually make us rush.
Use short pauses instead of filler words.
Look at one person per thought, and include every part of the room.
Keep gestures open and visible; plant your feet and move with purpose.
Sitting or standing, sit or stand tall and stay visible to your audience.

cards.prompt: Record yourself giving the first minute of a talk. Watch it once with the sound off and once without the picture. What is the one habit you will work on first?

quiz.question: What usually happens to speaking pace when someone is nervous?
options: It always slows to a stop
It stays exactly the same
It gets faster
It becomes perfectly even
quiz.explanation: Nerves usually make people speak too quickly. Deliberately slowing down for key lines helps the audience follow.

quiz.question: Which is a filler word?
options: 'Finally'
'First'
'However'
'Um'
quiz.explanation: Fillers such as 'um', 'uh', 'like' and 'basically' fill silence without adding meaning. Signposts like 'first' and 'finally' guide the audience.

quiz.question: What is a good guide for eye contact in a room?
options: Look at the ceiling so you do not get distracted
Stare at one friendly face for the whole talk so you feel more relaxed
Look at one person per thought, then move to someone else
Look only at your slides
quiz.explanation: Holding eye contact with one person for a sentence, then moving on, makes everyone feel included without anyone feeling stared at.

quiz.question: Where should your gestures usually be?
options: Hidden behind your back
Locked together in front of your stomach to keep them still and calm
Visible, roughly between your waist and shoulders
Mostly above your head
quiz.explanation: Gestures in this zone look natural and are easy for the audience to see. Hidden or locked hands can look tense.

quiz.question: Nadia sways from side to side as she speaks. What is the best fix?
options: Plant both feet; move, stop, then speak
Hold the back of a chair tightly so her body cannot move at all
Speak faster so the talk ends sooner
Stand on one leg to stay still
quiz.explanation: Planting both feet gives a steady base. Purposeful movement between points is fine; constant swaying distracts.

quiz.question: Why might a pause before a key line help?
options: It shows the audience you have forgotten your place
It builds attention so the line stands out
It gives you time to check your phone
It always makes the talk too long
quiz.explanation: A short pause signals that something important is coming and gives listeners a moment to focus.

quiz.question: Which habit fits presenting while sitting in a meeting?
options: Lean far back with arms crossed to look relaxed and in control
Sit tall near the front of the chair, hands above the table
Spin the chair gently while speaking
Keep hands in your lap under the table
quiz.explanation: Sitting tall and keeping gestures visible shows interest and confidence. Leaning back or hiding your hands can look disengaged.

quiz.question: In the 'energy and control' matrix, a speaker with a quiet voice and eyes on the floor is:
options: Engaging: high energy and high control
Restless: high energy and low control
Steady but flat: low energy and high control
Hidden: low energy and low control
quiz.explanation: Low energy and low control together make a speaker seem hidden. The aim is energy used with control.

quiz.question: Maryam must speak at a fixed microphone on a podium. What is the best approach?
options: Walk away from the microphone so she looks more natural and relaxed to the room
Stay at the microphone, stand slightly aside, relax, look up
Hide fully behind the podium and read
Ask to skip her turn
quiz.explanation: She must stay audible, but she can still show more of herself, free her hands and keep good eye contact.

quiz.question: When watching a recording of your practice, what is the most useful approach?
options: Fix every habit at once before the next run so the talk is perfect
Delete the video so it does not shake your confidence
Watch only the parts you liked
Pick one habit to improve and check it again next round
quiz.explanation: Improving one habit at a time is realistic and builds steady progress. Trying to fix everything at once is overwhelming.

sessions.title: Designing Clear Slides and Telling Stories with Data
sessions.summary: Step up to professional slides: one idea per slide, headline titles, visuals instead of walls of text, and charts that make numbers simple. Then learn to wrap your data in a short story so decision-makers remember it. Your win: a rebuilt five-slide deck with a clear story.
objectives: Design slides with one idea each and a headline that states the point
Replace bullet-heavy text with visuals, short phrases and speaker notes
Choose the right simple chart and highlight the one number that matters
Build a short story arc of situation, problem, action and result around your data
Make slides readable for everyone, including in large rooms and on small screens

cards.title: The wall of text
cards.setting: A sales office in Karachi, two days before the regional review.

lines.text: Usman's team leader has asked him to present last quarter's water filter sales to the regional manager. He shows Imran his draft on a video call.
I have put everything in. Slide four has eleven bullet points and two tables, so nobody can say I missed anything.
If the regional manager reads slide four, who is listening to you?
Nobody, I suppose. But if I remove the details, will it not look like I did less work?
The work shows in how clear it is. Slides are for the audience's eyes; the details live in your notes and a handout. One idea per slide, and every title tells the point.
So instead of 'Q3 Sales', the title says 'Office sales grew; home sales were flat'? That actually tells the story.

scenes.heading: One idea per slide
scenes.narration: Each slide should make a single point. If you need two points, use two slides. More slides with less on each is often clearer than a few crowded ones.

scenes.heading: Headline titles
scenes.narration: Write the title as a short sentence that states the point, like a newspaper headline, instead of a label such as 'Results'.

scenes.heading: Visuals over text
scenes.narration: Use a photo, a simple diagram or a chart where you can. Keep text to a few words, and say the rest out loud.

scenes.heading: Data made simple
scenes.narration: Show only the numbers that matter, choose a simple chart, and highlight the one bar or line you are talking about.

scenes.heading: Story around data
scenes.narration: Numbers alone are easy to forget. Explain the situation, the problem, what you did and the result.

cards.title: From data to a clear slide
cards.caption: Work in this order so the chart answers a question instead of just showing numbers.

items.label: Ask the question
items.detail: What does the audience need to know? For example, 'Which product line is growing?'

items.label: Find the answer
items.detail: Look at the data and write the answer in one sentence.

items.label: Pick the chart
items.detail: Bar to compare items, line for change over time, table for exact values.

items.label: Remove clutter
items.detail: Delete extra gridlines, 3D effects, legends you do not need and decimal places.

items.label: Highlight
items.detail: Use one strong colour for the key bar or line and grey for the rest.

items.label: Write the headline
items.detail: Put the one-sentence answer as the slide title.

cards.question: Which slide title is strongest for Usman's sales review?
options: Q3 Sales
Sales Data Table (see below)
Office filter sales grew this quarter, home sales stayed flat
Some Numbers From Our Department
cards.explanation: A headline title states the point so the audience understands the slide at a glance. Labels like 'Q3 Sales' make them work out the meaning themselves.

cards.title: Choosing the right chart
cards.body:
Match the chart to the question you are answering:

| Question | Good choice |
|---|---|
| Which item is biggest or smallest? | Bar chart |
| How did something change over time? | Line chart |
| What share of one whole does each part take? | A simple bar, or a pie with very few parts |
| What are the exact figures? | A small table |

Keep it simple: no 3D effects, few colours, labels written directly on the bars or lines where possible, and round numbers when exact decimals do not matter. Always check that the axis starts at a sensible point, because a cut-off axis can make a small change look huge, which can mislead people.

cards.title: Match the data question to the chart
cards.prompt: Match each question to the chart that answers it best.

pairs.left: How did monthly orders change over a year?
pairs.right: Line chart

pairs.left: Which of five branches sold the most?
pairs.right: Bar chart

pairs.left: What are the exact prices of four packages?
pairs.right: Small table

pairs.left: Is one product line far ahead of the other two?
pairs.right: Bar chart with the leader highlighted

pairs.left: How do last year and this year compare, month by month?
pairs.right: Two lines on one line chart

cards.title: Crowded slide versus clear slide
cards.caption: The same information, designed for a listening audience.

items.label: Title
items.left: 'Q3 Sales'
items.right: 'Office sales grew; home sales were flat'

items.label: Text
items.left: Eleven bullet points in small font
items.right: A few words; the detail is spoken

items.label: Data
items.left: Two full tables with every figure
items.right: One bar chart with the key bar highlighted

items.label: Speaker
items.left: Reads the slide aloud with back to the room
items.right: Faces the audience and explains the point

items.label: Details
items.left: All on screen at once
items.right: In speaker notes and a handout sent afterwards

cards.title: The supervisor wants everything
cards.situation: Maryam's supervisor says, 'Make sure every test result is on your slides.' She has 15 minutes and 40 rows of results. If she puts them all on screen, the examiners will be reading tables instead of listening.

choices.text: Show one clear chart of the main result, put the full table in an appendix slide and a printed handout, and tell her supervisor the plan.
choices.outcome: The examiners follow her story, and when one asks about a specific test, she opens the appendix in seconds. Her supervisor is happy that nothing is missing.

choices.text: Put all 40 rows on two slides in very small font.
choices.outcome: Nobody can read the numbers from their seats. She spends minutes saying 'you can see here...' while people squint.

choices.text: Leave out the table completely without telling anyone.
choices.outcome: The slides are clear, but when the examiners ask for detail she has nothing to show, and her supervisor feels ignored.

cards.title: On the slide or in the notes?
cards.prompt: Sort each item by where it belongs in a talk to a listening audience.

items.text: A headline title stating the point
One chart with the key number highlighted
A strong photo of the product in use
Full table of 40 test results
The exact wording of everything you will say
Long definitions and references
Three or four short phrases
Background history of the department

cards.title: A simple story arc for data
cards.caption: Wrap your numbers in a story your audience can follow and retell.

items.label: Situation
items.detail: Where things stood: 'Home and office sales were growing at the same pace.'

items.label: Problem
items.detail: What changed: 'This quarter, home sales stopped growing.'

items.label: Action
items.detail: What was done or should be done: 'We visited twenty home customers to ask why.'

items.label: Result
items.detail: What happened or will happen: 'Most wanted easier filter changes, so we suggest a home service plan.'

cards.question: Usman's chart has 3D bars, six colours and a legend. He wants the audience to see that office sales grew. What is the best change?
options: Use flat bars, grey for most and one strong colour for office sales
Add more colours so each bar looks different
Make the chart smaller so it fits beside more bullet points
Add a second legend to explain the first one
cards.explanation: Removing clutter and highlighting the key bar guides the eye straight to the point. Extra colours and effects compete for attention.

cards.title: Nadia's data story
cards.body:
Nadia wants an office in Faisalabad to switch from a large caterer to her lunches. Instead of a slide full of numbers, she tells a short story (all figures here are from her own fictional records):

- **Situation:** 'Last spring, I started delivering to one small office of twelve people.'
- **Problem:** 'Their old supplier was often late, so staff were eating at their desks after 2 pm.'
- **Action:** 'We set a 12:30 delivery window and sent a message when the rider left.'
- **Result:** 'Over three months, every delivery but two arrived inside the window, and the office has now renewed for a year.'

One simple bar chart shows on-time deliveries by month. The story makes the chart matter.

cards.title: Make slides readable for everyone
cards.body:
- Use a large font: if you have to squint at your laptop from two steps back, it is too small.
- Use strong contrast: dark text on a light background, or the reverse.
- Do not rely on colour alone: some people cannot tell red from green, so add labels or patterns.
- Avoid text over busy photos.
- Test your slides on the real screen if you can, and on a phone if people will join online.

In PowerPoint on Windows, **F5** starts the show from the first slide, and pressing **B** during the show turns the screen black so all eyes come to you; press **B** again to bring the slide back. Other apps have similar options, so check their help pages.

cards.back: A slide title written as a short sentence that states the point.
Private notes under each slide that you can see, but the audience cannot, in presenter view.
Extra detail placed after your closing slide, ready if someone asks.
One strong colour used only for the thing you want people to notice.
Decoration that adds nothing: 3D effects, heavy gridlines, shadows and clip art.
A document with full details, shared before or after the talk, so slides can stay simple.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Slide Studio
items: One idea per slide, with a headline title that states the point.
Use visuals and a few words; say the detail and keep it in notes or a handout.
Pick the simplest chart for the question, remove clutter and highlight one thing.
Wrap data in a story: situation, problem, action, result.
Check readability: large font, strong contrast and not relying on colour alone.

cards.prompt: Open a deck you have used before. Choose one crowded slide. What is its single point, and how would you redesign it with a headline title and one visual?

quiz.question: What does 'one idea per slide' mean?
options: A deck should have only one slide
Each slide makes a single point
Each slide must have one bullet point
Only one person may present the slides
quiz.explanation: Each slide should carry one clear point. If you have two points, use two slides.

quiz.question: Which is a headline title?
options: 'Results'
'Slide 7'
'Data'
'Home sales stopped growing this quarter'
quiz.explanation: A headline title states the point as a short sentence. Labels like 'Results' or 'Data' do not tell the audience what to conclude.

quiz.question: Which chart best shows how monthly orders changed over a year?
options: Line chart
Pie chart
A table of 365 rows
3D cone chart
quiz.explanation: Line charts show change over time clearly. Pies show parts of a whole, and huge tables are hard to read on a slide.

quiz.question: Where should the full table of 40 test results go in a 15-minute talk?
options: In an appendix slide and a handout
On the title slide
On every slide in small text
Nowhere, and deny it exists if asked
quiz.explanation: Keeping full detail in an appendix and handout keeps the main slides clear while still making the data available.

quiz.question: Why should you check where a chart's axis starts?
options: Axes must always start at 100, or the chart software shows an error
It changes the colours of the bars
A cut-off axis can make a small change look much bigger
It decides how many slides you need
quiz.explanation: Starting the axis far above zero can exaggerate differences and mislead the audience. Honest charts build trust.

quiz.question: Usman wants the audience to notice one bar. What is the best design choice?
options: Give every bar a different bright colour so each one stands out clearly
Add a 3D shadow to all bars
Colour that bar strongly and make the others grey
Make the chart as small as possible
quiz.explanation: Using one highlight colour against neutral grey guides the eye to the key point straight away.

quiz.question: What are the four parts of the simple data story arc in this stage?
options: Title, bullets, chart, thank you
Situation, problem, action, result
Opening, joke, quiz, ending
Past, present, future, appendix
quiz.explanation: Situation, problem, action and result give numbers a context that audiences can follow and remember.

quiz.question: Why should you not rely on colour alone in a chart?
options: Projectors cannot show colour
Colour is never allowed on slides
Some people cannot tell certain colours apart
Colour makes the file too large to send by email after the talk
quiz.explanation: Some viewers have colour vision differences, so labels or patterns help everyone read the chart.

quiz.question: In PowerPoint on Windows, what does pressing B during a slide show do?
options: Goes back to the first slide
Closes the presentation file
Turns the screen black until B is pressed again
Makes the text bold
quiz.explanation: Pressing B in slide show mode blacks out the screen so attention comes to the speaker. Pressing B again returns to the slide.

quiz.question: Maryam's supervisor insists every result must be included. What best balances clarity and his request?
options: All 40 results on screen in very small text so the supervisor sees everything
A clear chart in the talk; full results in an appendix and handout
Remove the results and say nothing
Read every result aloud quickly
quiz.explanation: This keeps the talk easy to follow while making sure no result is missing, and it respects the supervisor's request.

sessions.title: Handling Questions, Tough Audiences, Time Limits and Mistakes
sessions.summary: The real test of a presenter comes when things do not go to plan. Learn a calm method for answering any question, ways to handle challengers and silent rooms, how to cut a talk when time is short, and how to recover from mistakes without losing trust. Your win: a Q&A plan and a time plan for your next talk.
objectives: Answer questions with a calm listen, pause, rephrase, answer and check method
Respond to challenging, off-topic and long-winded questions politely and firmly
Plan time checkpoints and cut a talk quickly when your slot is shortened
Recover from mistakes and technical problems without losing the audience
Say 'I do not know' honestly and follow up in a professional way

cards.title: The price question
cards.setting: A school meeting room in Faisalabad, after Nadia's lunch proposal.

lines.text: Nadia has just finished her talk to the school's admin committee. Then the questions begin.
Thank you. I am happy to take any questions.
A committee member folds his arms. He says her price is higher than the canteen's and asks why the school should pay more. Nadia freezes, then talks very fast about her recipes.
That evening, Imran calls her to hear how it went.
You knew the answer, Nadia. What happened?
It felt like an attack. I wanted to defend everything at once.
Next time, listen to the end, pause, repeat the question in calm words, then answer the real worry: value for the price. Short, honest and calm wins the room.

scenes.heading: Listen fully
scenes.narration: Let the person finish. Do not plan your answer while they are still talking, and do not interrupt.

scenes.heading: Pause
scenes.narration: Take a breath. A short pause shows you are thinking, not panicking.

scenes.heading: Rephrase
scenes.narration: Repeat the question in neutral words: 'So the question is how our price compares with the canteen.' This helps everyone hear it and takes the heat out.

scenes.heading: Answer briefly
scenes.narration: Give your main point first, one reason or example, and stop. Long answers often create new doubts.

scenes.heading: Check and move on
scenes.narration: Ask 'Does that answer your question?' and then look to the rest of the room for the next one.

cards.title: The answer cycle
cards.caption: Use the same calm steps for easy and hard questions alike.

items.label: Listen
items.detail: Hear the whole question and the worry behind it.

items.label: Pause
items.detail: Breathe; take a moment to think.

items.label: Rephrase
items.detail: Repeat it calmly so everyone hears it.

items.label: Answer
items.detail: Main point first, one reason, then stop.

items.label: Check
items.detail: Confirm it helped, then open the floor again.

cards.question: A committee member says, 'Your price is too high.' What is the best first move?
options: Listen to the end, pause, and rephrase the concern calmly
Interrupt quickly to defend every part of the menu
Say that the canteen's food is bad
Ignore the comment and move to the next slide
cards.explanation: Listening fully, pausing and rephrasing shows respect and gives you time to find the real worry, which is usually value for money.

cards.title: Four tough audience moments
cards.body:
- **The challenger:** someone disagrees strongly. Stay calm, thank them for raising it, find the part you agree with, then give your evidence. Never argue about who is right in front of the room.
- **The long talker:** someone makes a speech instead of asking. Wait for a breath, then say kindly, 'Thank you. What is the question you would most like me to answer?'
- **The off-topic question:** 'That is a good point, but outside today's topic. Can we talk about it after the session?' Then really follow up.
- **The silent room:** nobody asks. Prepare a starter: 'A question I often hear is...' Or ask them a simple question first.

If you do not know the answer, say so: 'I do not know, but I will find out and email you by Thursday.' Then do it. Guessing damages trust far more than honesty.

cards.title: Tough moment, steady response
cards.prompt: Match each difficult moment to a strong response.

pairs.left: A question you cannot answer
pairs.right: 'I do not know yet. I will check and send it to you by Thursday.'

pairs.left: An off-topic question
pairs.right: 'Good point; it is outside today's topic. Can we discuss it after the session?'

pairs.left: A long speech with no clear question
pairs.right: 'Thank you. What is the main question you would like me to answer?'

pairs.left: A strong challenge to your data
pairs.right: 'Thank you for raising that. Here is where the figures come from.'

pairs.left: A silent room after your talk
pairs.right: 'A question I often hear is about cost, so let me start there.'

cards.title: Reacting versus responding
cards.caption: Under pressure, choose a response instead of a reflex.

items.label: First second
items.left: Interrupts or starts defending at once
items.right: Listens to the end and pauses

items.label: Tone
items.left: Sharp, fast and louder
items.right: Calm, steady and warm

items.label: Content
items.left: Long answer covering everything
items.right: Main point, one reason, then stop

items.label: Not knowing
items.left: Guesses or bluffs
items.right: Says so honestly and promises a follow-up

items.label: Afterwards
items.left: Avoids eye contact with the questioner
items.right: Checks it helped and moves on

cards.title: Twenty minutes becomes eight
cards.situation: Usman is waiting to present a new service plan to the regional manager. The meeting has overrun, and the chairperson says, 'Sorry, Usman, you have eight minutes, not twenty.' His deck has fourteen slides.

choices.text: Say his key message first, cover his three points using only the key slides, and close with his request, keeping the rest for questions.
choices.outcome: He finishes in seven minutes with a clear ask. The manager asks two questions, and Usman uses two of the skipped slides to answer them. He gets approval for a trial.

choices.text: Present all fourteen slides at double speed.
choices.outcome: He rushes, stumbles and runs over time. The manager remembers the rush, not the plan.

choices.text: Ask to move his slot to the next meeting in a month.
choices.outcome: It is a safe choice, but he loses the chance while the manager is in the room. Sometimes this is needed, but here he was ready.

cards.title: A ten-minute talk with checkpoints
cards.caption: Know where you should be at each point, and what you can cut if you are behind.

items.label: Minute 0 to 1
items.detail: Hook, key message and map.

items.label: Minute 1 to 4
items.detail: Point one, with one example.

items.label: Minute 4 to 6
items.detail: Point two. If you are behind here, use the short version of point three.

items.label: Minute 6 to 8
items.detail: Point three.

items.label: Minute 8 to 9
items.detail: Summary and call to action.

items.label: Minute 9 to 10
items.detail: Buffer for a late start or a question.

cards.title: Recover from a mistake
cards.prompt: Put these steps for recovering from a slip or a technical problem in order.
steps: Pause and take one slow breath
Acknowledge it briefly if needed, for example 'Let me correct that figure'
Give the correct information or switch to your backup
Return to your structure with a signpost, such as 'So, my second point...'
Carry on without apologising again

cards.title: Strong or weak way to handle questions?
cards.prompt: Sort each habit by how well it handles questions.

items.text: Rephrasing the question so everyone hears it
Interrupting before the person finishes
Saying 'I do not know, I will follow up by Friday'
Guessing a number to avoid looking unsure
Giving the main point first and then stopping
Arguing with a challenger until they give up
Preparing answers to likely tough questions in advance
Saying 'That is a stupid question'

cards.question: During her talk, Maryam realises she gave the wrong number on an earlier slide. What should she do?
options: Ignore it and hope nobody noticed
Correct it briefly and calmly, then carry on with her structure
Apologise several times and start the talk again
Blame the software for changing the number
cards.explanation: A quick, calm correction keeps trust. Hiding errors or making a big fuss both damage credibility more than the mistake itself.

cards.title: Maryam and the external examiner
cards.body:
At her final-year project presentation, an external examiner says, 'Ten classmates is too small a test. Your results mean nothing.'

Maryam's heart races, but she uses the cycle. She listens to the end. She pauses. Then she says: 'So the concern is whether a test with ten users is enough to trust the results.'

She answers: 'You are right that it is small. It was a first test to find usability problems, not to prove the app works for everyone. That is why our next step is a trial with the whole library.'

She agrees with the fair part, explains the purpose, and links back to her call to action. The examiner nods and writes something down.

cards.title: Prepare for the hot seat
cards.body:
- List the five hardest questions someone could ask you, and practise short answers out loud.
- Ask a friend to play a tough audience member.
- Keep backup slides with extra detail after your closing slide.
- Carry your talk in two formats, such as a file on a USB drive and a copy in your email or cloud drive, and a printed outline in case the screen fails.
- Mark two time checkpoints in your notes and decide in advance what you will cut if you are behind.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Hot Seat
items: Use the answer cycle: listen, pause, rephrase, answer briefly, check.
Stay calm with challengers, agree with what is fair, then give evidence.
Say 'I do not know' honestly and follow up when you promised.
Plan time checkpoints and know what you will cut if time is short.
Correct mistakes briefly, return to your structure and carry on.

cards.prompt: Write down the toughest question someone could ask about your next talk. How would you answer it in three sentences, using the answer cycle?

quiz.question: What is the first step when someone asks you a question?
options: Start answering as soon as you guess it
Listen to the whole question
Look at your next slide
Thank them and move on
quiz.explanation: Listening fully shows respect and helps you understand the real concern before you answer.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to rephrase a question before answering?
options: It makes the answer sound longer and more detailed than it really is
It avoids answering the question
It shows you did not understand it
It helps everyone hear it and calms the tone
quiz.explanation: Rephrasing in neutral words ensures everyone heard the question, gives you time to think and lowers any tension.

quiz.question: What should you do if you do not know the answer?
options: Guess a number so you look confident
Say so, and promise a specific follow-up
Change the subject quickly
Say the question is not important
quiz.explanation: Honesty with a clear follow-up keeps your credibility. Guessing can be exposed later and damage trust.

quiz.question: Someone gives a long speech instead of asking a question. What is a polite, firm response?
options: 'Please stop talking now.'
Wait silently until they give up and sit down
'Thank you. What is your main question?'
Start the next slide while they talk
quiz.explanation: This thanks them, then guides them to a clear question so you can answer and keep the session on track.

quiz.question: Usman's slot is cut from twenty minutes to eight. What is the best plan?
options: Show all slides at double speed
Skip the call to action to save time
Give the key message, three points on key slides and the request
Spend the time explaining why the cut is unfair to him and his team
quiz.explanation: When time is cut, keep the structure and the ask, and drop detail. Rushing everything loses the audience.

quiz.question: Why should you leave a short buffer at the end of a timed talk?
options: So you can show extra slides at the end
Because audiences prefer silence
So the next speaker can start early
To absorb a late start, a slip or a question
quiz.explanation: A buffer protects your close and call to action if something takes longer than planned.

quiz.question: An audience member strongly challenges your data. Which response is best?
options: Thank them, agree with the fair part, then give evidence calmly
Argue firmly until they admit in front of the whole room that they are wrong
Say they clearly did not listen
Ignore them and take another question
quiz.explanation: Calmly acknowledging the point and then giving evidence shows confidence and respect, and keeps the room on your side.

quiz.question: The projector fails five minutes into your talk. What is the best response?
options: Stop and wait quietly for the projector to be fixed before saying anything
Apologise repeatedly while trying to fix it
Pause, switch to your printed outline and continue your structure
Cancel the talk
quiz.explanation: A prepared backup lets you keep going. Your structure, not your slides, carries the talk.

quiz.question: After answering a question, what is a good final step?
options: Check it helped, then look to the room for the next question
Ask the person to sit down quickly
Repeat the answer twice more
Move straight to a brand-new topic without pausing or checking anything
quiz.explanation: Checking shows care, and opening the floor again keeps the session moving.

quiz.question: Nobody asks a question after your talk. What can you do?
options: End immediately and leave the room
Tell the audience they are not paying attention
Ask the organiser to pick someone
Start with 'A question I often hear is...' and answer it
quiz.explanation: A prepared starter question breaks the silence and often encourages others to ask.

sessions.title: Presenting Online and in High-Stakes Settings, Plus Your Practice Plan
sessions.summary: Bring everything together for the moments that matter most: video-call presentations, pitches to clients or management, panels and interview presentation tasks. Then build a feedback-and-practice plan so you keep improving after this course. Your win: a four-week practice plan.
objectives: Set up camera, light, sound and screen sharing for a professional video presentation
Keep online audiences engaged with eye contact to camera and regular interaction
Structure a pitch to a client or management around their problem and a clear ask
Prepare for panels and interview presentation tasks
Build a feedback-and-practice plan with specific goals

cards.title: Two big days
cards.setting: A video call between Lahore, Karachi and Islamabad, Sunday evening.

lines.text: On Wednesday I pitch our office service plan to a client's management team on a video call. If my internet drops, it is over.
And on Thursday I have a job interview in Lahore. They want a ten-minute presentation on a project, then a panel will ask questions.
You have both come a long way. The basics stay the same: audience, one message, structure, voice and calm answers. High stakes just mean more preparation.
But online is different. I cannot see if people are bored.
So you build in interaction, look at the camera and test everything the day before. And you have a backup plan for the internet. Let us make a checklist for each of you.
And after Thursday, a plan to keep practising, so this does not stop when the course ends.

scenes.heading: Set up for video
scenes.narration: Camera at eye level, light in front of you, a quiet room and a headset or good microphone. Test the link, the screen share and your sound the day before.

scenes.heading: Connect through the screen
scenes.narration: Look at the camera when you make a key point, not at your own face. Name people, ask a question or run a quick poll every few minutes.

scenes.heading: Pitch to decision-makers
scenes.narration: Lead with their problem and your recommendation, then the benefits, the cost and the risks, and finish with a clear ask.

scenes.heading: Panels and interviews
scenes.narration: Keep answers short, connect your points to the role or topic, and listen to the other speakers or panel members.

scenes.heading: Keep improving
scenes.narration: Plan, practise, record, get specific feedback and adjust. Small, regular practice beats one big effort before each talk.

cards.title: In the room versus on a video call
cards.caption: The same skills, adjusted for the screen.

items.label: Eye contact
items.left: Look at people around the room
items.right: Look at the camera for key points

items.label: Energy
items.left: Natural room energy helps you
items.right: Add a little more energy to your voice and face

items.label: Interaction
items.left: Read faces and ask as you go
items.right: Plan a question, poll or chat prompt every few minutes

items.label: Slides
items.left: Visible on a big screen
items.right: Larger text; share one window, not your whole desktop

items.label: Backup
items.left: Printed outline and a USB copy
items.right: Phone hotspot, dial-in or a co-host who can share the slides

cards.question: Usman wants online viewers to feel he is speaking to them. Where should he look when he makes his key point?
options: At the camera
At his own video tile
At his notes on the desk
At the chat window the whole time
cards.explanation: Looking into the camera is how online viewers feel eye contact. Glancing at notes or faces between points is fine.

cards.title: Pitching to clients or management
cards.body:
Decision-makers are busy. They want to know quickly what you recommend and why. A clear pitch often follows this order:

1. **Their problem:** 'Your staff lose time arranging drinking water every week.'
2. **Your recommendation:** 'A monthly filter service plan for your two offices.'
3. **Benefits:** what changes for them, in their terms.
4. **Cost and effort:** be open about what it takes.
5. **Risks and how you handle them:** this builds trust.
6. **The ask:** 'Can we start a one-month trial on 1 December?'

Prepare for the questions decision-makers usually ask: cost, time, risk, proof and 'What happens if it does not work?'. Keep pricing honest and check your figures before you present.

cards.back: Answer the exact brief, keep to the time, and link your talk to the job you are applying for.
Look at the person who asked, then include the others as you finish your answer.
Keep each answer short, build on what others said, and avoid taking more than your share of time.
Pause, rephrase, and answer what you can. It is fine to take a moment to think.
Agree the order and timing beforehand, and watch for their signals to wrap up.
Thank the organisers and follow up on any promises within the time you said.

cards.title: Your feedback-and-practice cycle
cards.caption: Repeat this cycle for every important talk, and in small practice sessions between them.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Set one or two specific goals, such as fewer fillers or a stronger close.

items.label: Practise
items.detail: Run the talk out loud in short rounds.

items.label: Record
items.detail: Video yourself, or ask a friend to watch.

items.label: Get feedback
items.detail: Ask specific questions, not 'Was it okay?'

items.label: Adjust
items.detail: Change one or two things and try again.

cards.title: The frozen screen
cards.situation: Ten minutes into Usman's video-call pitch, his internet becomes unstable. His video freezes and his voice cuts in and out. The client's manager types in the chat: 'We can't hear you clearly.'

choices.text: Turn his camera off to save bandwidth, switch to his phone hotspot or dial-in, and ask his colleague, who has a copy of the slides, to share them while he continues.
choices.outcome: Within a minute he is back, clear and calm. The client sees a well-prepared team, and the pitch carries on with his key message intact.

choices.text: Keep talking and hope the connection improves.
choices.outcome: The client misses most of his main point and stops paying attention. Several people go off camera.

choices.text: Apologise in the chat and ask to reschedule for next week.
choices.outcome: It is polite, and sometimes necessary, but the momentum is lost. A tested backup would have saved the pitch.

cards.title: Online set-up: do or avoid?
cards.prompt: Sort each habit for a video presentation.

items.text: Camera at eye level
A bright window behind you
Test sound and screen share the day before
Share your whole desktop with messages popping up
Turn off notifications before you start
Look at your own video tile while speaking
Plan a question or poll every few minutes
Read your slides word for word

cards.title: Prepare for an interview presentation
cards.prompt: Put these steps for Maryam's interview presentation in a sensible order.
steps: Read the brief carefully and note the time limit and topic
Research the organisation and link the topic to the role
Choose one key message and three points
Build a few clear slides, if slides are allowed
Practise aloud with a timer and record one run
Prepare short answers to likely panel questions
On the day, arrive early and check the room or link

cards.question: Which feedback question will help Maryam improve most after a practice run?
options: 'Was it okay?'
'What was one moment where I lost you, and why?'
'Did you like it?'
'Was I better than the others?'
cards.explanation: Specific questions get specific, useful feedback. Vague questions usually get polite answers that do not help you improve.

cards.title: Maryam's four-week practice plan
cards.body:
After her interview, Maryam writes a simple plan to keep improving:

- **Week 1:** Record a two-minute talk on any topic. Goal: fewer fillers. Count them.
- **Week 2:** Present a short update in her study group. Goal: a stronger hook. Ask one friend for feedback.
- **Week 3:** Volunteer to answer questions after a group presentation. Goal: use the answer cycle every time.
- **Week 4:** Give a five-minute talk on a video call to friends. Goal: look at the camera for key points.

She keeps short notes after each one: what went well, one thing to change. She does not aim for perfect; she aims for a little better each time.

cards.title: Ask for feedback that helps
cards.body:
