Give your listener a focus before you start, for example 'Please watch my pace and my close.' Then ask:

- 'What was the one main message you took away?'
- 'Where did you lose attention, if anywhere?'
- 'What is one thing I should keep, and one thing I should change?'

Thank people for honest feedback, even if it stings. If their main message is not the one you intended, your structure needs work, not your confidence.

cards.title: High-stakes setting, best habit
cards.prompt: Match each setting to a habit that helps most.

pairs.left: Video-call pitch
pairs.right: Test the link and screen share the day before, with a backup ready

pairs.left: Pitch to management
pairs.right: Lead with the recommendation and finish with a clear ask

pairs.left: Discussion panel
pairs.right: Keep answers short and build on what others said

pairs.left: Interview presentation
pairs.right: Answer the exact brief and link it to the role

pairs.left: After any big talk
pairs.right: Note what went well and one thing to change

cards.title: Take-aways from the Big Room
items: Online: camera at eye level, light in front, tested sound and a backup plan.
Look at the camera for key points and build in interaction every few minutes.
Pitch with their problem, your recommendation, benefits, cost, risks and a clear ask.
In panels and interviews, answer the brief, keep it short and include everyone.
Keep improving with a cycle of plan, practise, record, feedback and adjust.

cards.prompt: Write your own four-week practice plan. For each week, choose one setting, one specific goal and one person you will ask for feedback.

quiz.question: Where should your camera be for a video presentation?
options: Roughly at eye level
Far below your chin
Pointing at the ceiling
Behind you
quiz.explanation: A camera at eye level gives a natural, face-to-face view, like sitting across a table.

quiz.question: Where is the best place for the main light when you are on camera?
options: Directly behind you
In front of you, facing you
Only above your head
No light at all
quiz.explanation: Light in front of you lights your face clearly. A bright window behind you turns you into a dark shape.

quiz.question: Why share one window instead of your whole desktop?
options: So private messages and notifications do not appear
Because desktops cannot be shared
It makes the internet faster for everyone who is on the call with you
So the audience cannot see your slides
quiz.explanation: Sharing only the window you need protects privacy and avoids embarrassing pop-ups.

quiz.question: How can you keep an online audience engaged?
options: Speak without stopping for the whole time
Turn off your camera so they focus only on the slides and your voice
Add more text to each slide
Plan a question, poll or chat prompt every few minutes
quiz.explanation: Regular interaction gives online viewers a reason to stay focused and lets you check understanding.

quiz.question: In a pitch to management, what should usually come early?
options: Your full company history
Their problem and your recommendation
Every technical detail
A long list of thank-yous
quiz.explanation: Decision-makers want the point quickly: what problem you solve and what you recommend.

quiz.question: Why should a pitch include the risks and how you will handle them?
options: It makes the pitch longer and more impressive
Being open about risks builds trust
Clients like to hear only bad news
It replaces the need for a clear ask
quiz.explanation: Decision-makers will think about risks anyway. Raising them yourself, with a plan, shows honesty and preparation.

quiz.question: In an interview presentation, what matters most?
options: Using as many slides as possible
Talking about your hobbies in detail
Answering the exact brief within the time limit
Speaking for longer than the time allowed
quiz.explanation: Interviewers set a brief to see if you can follow it, communicate clearly and link ideas to the role.

quiz.question: On a discussion panel, which habit helps most?
options: Take as much time as you can for each answer
Disagree with every other speaker
Read prepared paragraphs from your phone
Keep answers short and build on others' points
quiz.explanation: Good panellists share time, listen and connect their points to the discussion.

quiz.question: Usman's internet fails during a pitch. Which backup is most helpful?
options: A second laptop running on the same broken connection, ready to switch
A longer apology message
A plan to speak faster when it returns
A phone hotspot plus a colleague with a copy of the slides
quiz.explanation: A different connection and a co-host who can share the slides let the pitch continue with minimal disruption.

quiz.question: What makes a feedback request most useful?
options: Asking about a specific part, such as your close or pace
Asking 'Was it okay?'
Asking only the people who always praise you, so you stay confident
Asking after you have stopped practising
quiz.explanation: Specific questions get specific answers you can act on. Vague questions usually get polite but unhelpful replies.

bank.question: Two days before a talk, a speaker feels her heart race whenever she thinks about it. Which plan is most likely to help?
options: Avoid thinking about the talk until the morning it happens
Practise out loud in short rounds and breathe slowly
Add more slides so there is less she has to say
Memorise a full script word for word so she cannot go wrong on the day
bank.explanation: Familiarity from spoken practice and slow breathing both reduce nerves. Avoidance, extra slides and rigid scripts tend to make anxiety worse on the day.

bank.question: A trainer will present a new leave policy to factory supervisors who have little time and dislike long meetings. What should shape her talk first?
options: The full legal background of every rule, so nobody can question the policy
What they must do differently, and their limited time
Which slide theme looks most modern
How long the HR team spent writing the policy
bank.explanation: Audience analysis comes first: their need (what changes for them) and their limits (time). That decides what to include and what to leave in a handout.

bank.question: Which of these is a key message rather than a topic?
options: Weekly meetings
Some thoughts about our weekly meetings, travel times and other options for next year
Meeting online saves each of us an hour of travel
Meeting options for next year
bank.explanation: A key message states a clear point the audience can remember and act on. The others only name an area to talk about.

bank.question: A student says, 'I don't need to know my audience. My slides are the same for everyone.' What is the strongest reply?
options: Different listeners need different words, examples and detail
Audiences only care about how the slides look
Knowing your audience matters only for sales pitches, not for classes or teams
It is fine, as long as the talk is long enough
bank.explanation: Audience level and needs decide jargon, examples and depth. Experts and beginners need different versions of the same content.

bank.question: Why is 'How can I help these people?' a more useful thought than 'What will they think of me?' before speaking?
options: It guarantees the audience will like the talk
It means you no longer need to practise
It moves attention from self-judgement to the audience's needs
It removes all the physical signs of nerves, so the audience sees none
bank.explanation: Focusing outward reduces self-consciousness and gives your talk purpose. It helps, but it does not replace preparation or remove nerves entirely.

bank.question: A speaker has one week to prepare a ten-minute talk. Which practice plan is best?
options: One long silent read-through the night before
Short spoken runs across the week, one recorded, one for a friend
Write the slides on the final day so they feel fresh
Practise only the opening many times and improvise the rest on the day
bank.explanation: Spread-out spoken practice, with recording and feedback, builds familiarity across the whole talk. Cramming or practising one part leaves gaps.

bank.question: Nadia has eight possible sections for a five-minute talk. Which is the best way to decide what stays?
options: Keep what supports her key message; hand out the rest
Keep the sections she enjoyed writing most
Keep all eight and spend under a minute on each so nothing is left out
Keep the sections with the most numbers
bank.explanation: The key message is the filter. Content that does not support it can be shared elsewhere, keeping the talk focused.

bank.question: Which opening is most likely to hold a room of new university students?
options: 'Good morning, I would like to thank the dean, the staff, the organisers and everyone else.'
'Sorry, I was told about this talk only yesterday.'
'Who here has waited more than twenty minutes for a campus bus?'
'Today I will talk about some transport things.'
bank.explanation: A question linked to the audience's own experience hooks attention. Long thank-yous, apologies and vague topics lose people early.

bank.question: A speaker's three points are 'cost', 'our office in Multan' and 'a joke about traffic'. What is the main weakness?
options: Three points is always too many
The points do not all support one key message
Jokes are never allowed in talks
Cities should not be named in talks
bank.explanation: Each main point should support the key message. Unrelated points make a talk feel like a list rather than an argument.

bank.question: Where in a talk is the call to action most effective?
options: Hidden in the middle of the second point
Only on a slide that nobody reads aloud
At the end, after a short summary of the message
In a separate email a month later
bank.explanation: A call to action works best after the summary, when the audience has the full picture and the message is fresh.

bank.question: A team update ends with: 'So that's everything, I think. Thanks.' Which change would improve it most?
options: Repeat the key message and ask for one specific decision
Add three more points before saying thanks so the talk feels complete
Speak the same ending more quietly
Show a slide with the word 'Questions?'
bank.explanation: A strong close sums up and gives a clear next step. Adding content or a 'Questions?' slide does not fix a missing message and action.

bank.question: Why say a one-line map such as 'I will cover the problem, the plan and the cost' near the start?
options: It lets you skip signposts later
Listeners can follow the structure and know what is coming
It proves the talk is long enough
It replaces the need for an opening hook, so you can start straight away
bank.explanation: A map sets expectations. You still need a hook before it and signposts during the talk.

bank.question: A speaker uses 'finally' three times during a talk. What is the likely effect?
options: The audience feels the talk is very well organised and easy to follow
It makes the call to action stronger
Listeners stop trusting it and lose track of the end
Nobody notices signpost words
bank.explanation: Signposts guide only if they are accurate. Repeating 'finally' confuses listeners about where the talk really ends.

bank.question: Maryam wants to open with a striking fact. She remembers a number from a video but cannot find the source. What should she do?
options: Use the number anyway and round it up so it sounds stronger
Say it is 'well known' so nobody asks
Put it in small print on the slide
Use a fact she can check, or choose another hook
bank.explanation: Facts used in a talk must be checkable. If she cannot verify it, she should use her own data or a different kind of hook.

bank.question: A speaker rushes through numbers on a sales slide. Which change helps the audience most?
options: Speak louder but at the same speed
Read the numbers twice as fast to save time
Hide the numbers and describe them vaguely
Slow down and pause after each key number
bank.explanation: Numbers need time to land. Slowing down and pausing gives listeners time to understand and remember them.

bank.question: A presenter counts 15 filler words in her first recording and 9 in her second. What is the most useful next goal?
options: Stop recording because it makes her more nervous every time she watches
Replace each filler with 'basically'
Speak faster so there is no space for fillers
Reduce them a little more by pausing, not aim for zero at once
bank.explanation: Steady, measurable improvement is realistic. Replacing fillers with pauses works better than speeding up or swapping one filler for another.

bank.question: In a large hall, faces at the back are hard to see. Which eye-contact approach works best?
options: Look only at the front row
Look at the back wall above everyone's heads so nobody feels stared at
Keep your eyes on your slides
Look towards small groups in different parts of the hall
bank.explanation: Looking towards groups across the hall keeps everyone included, even when individual faces are unclear.

bank.question: During a seated interview panel, a candidate leans back, crosses his arms and gestures under the table. What impression is he most likely to give?
options: Closed or uninterested, even if he means to be relaxed
Energetic and engaged, because relaxed posture always shows confidence
Highly prepared
Formal and respectful
bank.explanation: Body language is read before words. Sitting tall with visible gestures signals interest; leaning back with crossed arms can look closed.

bank.question: Which pair best describes a speaker in the 'restless' part of the energy and control matrix?
options: Fast speech and constant pacing
A quiet voice and eyes on the floor
Varied tone with purposeful pauses
Calm, even delivery with little expression
bank.explanation: Restless means high energy with low control. A quiet, hidden speaker has low energy; calm but flat speakers have control but low energy.

bank.question: A presenter moves while speaking. Which pattern looks most confident?
options: Keep walking back and forth for the whole talk
Step forward and back on every sentence
Turn his back to walk to the screen often
Walk to a new spot between points, stop, then speak
bank.explanation: Purposeful movement links to the structure and then stops. Constant movement distracts and can look nervous.

bank.question: A speaker notices her voice drops at the end of each sentence. What is the best fix?
options: Speak more quietly overall so the ends of sentences sound more even
Breathe before each sentence and keep volume to the last word
Shorten every sentence to two words
Use more filler words to fill the gaps
bank.explanation: Fading endings usually come from running out of breath. A fresh breath and steady volume keep key final words clear.

bank.question: A slide titled 'Q2 Results' shows four bars. The speaker's point is that the Hyderabad branch fell behind. Which change helps most?
options: Add a fifth bar for the national average
Change the bars to a 3D pie
Add a paragraph of explanation under the chart so the point is clear
Retitle it to state that point and highlight that bar
bank.explanation: A headline title plus one highlighted bar tells the audience the point at a glance. Extra data, 3D effects or paragraphs add clutter.

bank.question: Which question is best answered with a line chart?
options: Which of four products sold most last month?
What are the exact fees for three courses?
How did monthly website visits change across the year?
How many staff are in each department today?
bank.explanation: Line charts show change over time. Comparisons between categories suit bar charts, and exact values suit small tables.

bank.question: A chart's vertical axis starts at 95 instead of 0, so a change from 96 to 98 looks huge. What is the main risk?
options: The chart will not print correctly on most office printers
The colours become harder to read
It shows the speaker worked very hard
It can mislead the audience about the size of the change
bank.explanation: Cutting the axis can exaggerate small differences. Honest scales protect your credibility, especially with decision-makers.

bank.question: A manager says, 'Your slides look empty. Where is all the detail?' What is the best reply?
options: The detail is in my notes and handout; slides show key points
Detail is never needed in presentations
I will add all the detail in small font so nothing is missing from the slides
I ran out of time to finish the slides
bank.explanation: Slides for a listening audience carry key points; detail belongs in notes, appendix slides and handouts, which you can offer.

bank.question: Which sequence correctly follows the story arc for data used in this course?
options: Problem, result, situation, action
Situation, problem, action, result
Action, situation, result, problem
Result, action, problem, situation
bank.explanation: Situation sets the scene, the problem creates tension, the action shows what was done, and the result shows what changed.

bank.question: A chart uses red for 'late' and green for 'on time' with no labels. Why is this a problem?
options: Red and green cannot be shown on projectors
Charts may only use one colour
Some viewers cannot easily tell red from green
Labels always make charts harder to read
bank.explanation: Colour vision differences mean colour alone can fail. Adding labels or patterns makes the chart readable for everyone.

bank.question: A presenter has 12 minutes and 30 slides, each with one clear idea and a picture. Is this a problem?
options: Yes; a talk should never have more than ten slides, whatever its length
Yes; every slide must have at least five bullet points
No; slide count is the only thing that matters
Not necessarily; simple slides can work at a clear pace
bank.explanation: There is no fixed slide count. What matters is one idea per slide, a clear message and a pace that fits the time. Rehearsing with a timer is the real test.

bank.question: A client interrupts: 'This is too expensive.' Which response follows the answer cycle best?
options: Let him finish, pause, rephrase the concern, then answer briefly
Lower the price on the spot to keep him happy
Say the competitor's product is much worse
Tell him you will come to cost much later in the talk and move straight on
bank.explanation: Listening, pausing, rephrasing and a brief answer show respect and address the real concern without panic or blame.

bank.question: A speaker does not know the answer to a technical question. What is the most professional response?
options: Give a confident guess so the room stays calm and nobody doubts you
Say the question is not relevant
'I'm not sure. I'll check and email you by tomorrow.'
Say 'Nobody knows that' and move on
bank.explanation: Honesty with a specific follow-up protects trust. A wrong guess can damage credibility for the rest of the relationship.

bank.question: An audience member raises an off-topic issue that matters to him. What is the best response?
options: Thank him, offer to discuss it after, then follow up
Answer it fully, even if it takes half the remaining time
Say the issue is unimportant
Pretend not to hear and take another question
bank.explanation: Acknowledging the point and offering a real follow-up respects the person while protecting the session's purpose and time.

bank.question: A 15-minute talk is cut to 6 minutes as you stand up. What should stay no matter what?
options: The key message, short main points and the ask
Every slide, shown more quickly, so nothing is lost
The full introduction about yourself
The detailed method section
bank.explanation: When time is cut, protect the message and the ask. Detail can move to questions, appendix slides or a follow-up.

bank.question: Halfway through, a speaker realises a figure she gave earlier was wrong. Which approach is best?
options: Correct it briefly at once and continue with her structure
Wait until the end and hope nobody noticed
Stop and apologise many times
Change the figure on the slide quietly without mentioning it to anyone
bank.explanation: A quick, open correction keeps trust. Hiding errors or over-apologising draws more attention and harms credibility.

bank.question: A challenger says, 'Your sample of ten users proves nothing.' Which response is strongest?
options: Insist firmly that ten users is more than enough to prove the app works
Ask why he is trying to embarrass you
Agree it is small, explain its purpose, link to next steps
Ignore the point and show the next slide
bank.explanation: Agreeing with the fair part, explaining purpose and pointing to next steps is honest and confident, and it keeps the audience on your side.

bank.question: A speaker plans time checkpoints in a ten-minute talk. What is their main benefit?
options: They let her add extra content if she is early
They show early if she is behind, so she can cut as planned
They replace the need for practice
They make the talk last exactly ten minutes without any extra effort
bank.explanation: Checkpoints reveal timing problems while there is still time to adjust, using cuts decided in advance.

bank.question: On a video call, a presenter sits with a bright window behind him. What is the likely problem?
options: His face appears dark and hard to see
His voice will sound louder
The slides will not share
The call will end automatically
bank.explanation: Strong light behind you leaves your face in shadow. Light in front of you, or facing the window, solves it.

bank.question: Before an online pitch, which check is most important to do the day before?
options: Choose a new background image
Change the slide font to a new style
Change the slide font to a new style that looks better on camera
Test link, sound and screen share; have a backup
bank.explanation: Technical tests and a backup plan prevent the most common online failures. Visual tweaks matter far less.

bank.question: In a pitch to management, why should the recommendation usually come early?
options: It makes the pitch sound less prepared
Managers prefer surprises at the end
It allows you to skip the evidence
Busy decision-makers want the point quickly, then the reasons
bank.explanation: Leading with the recommendation respects decision-makers' time. The benefits, cost, risks and evidence then support it.

bank.question: During a panel interview, one panel member asks a question. Where should the candidate look while answering?
options: Only at the most senior person, since they make the final decision
At the asker, then the others as the answer ends
At the table to avoid seeming rude
At the door, to look calm
bank.explanation: Answering the questioner directly and then including the others shows respect for the whole panel.

bank.question: A friend says your practice talk was 'fine'. Which next question will give the most useful feedback?
options: 'So you liked it?'
'What was the one message you took away?'
'Was it better than last time?'
'Should I give up presenting?'
bank.explanation: If the message they heard differs from the one you intended, you know exactly what to work on. Yes-or-no questions rarely help.

bank.question: An interview brief asks for a 'ten-minute presentation on a process you improved'. A candidate prepares 20 minutes on her whole degree. What is the main risk?
options: Panels prefer longer talks, so there is no real risk in going over
She is off the brief and over time, which panels notice
She will have too few slides
She will finish too early
bank.explanation: Interview tasks test whether you can follow a brief and manage time. Going off-brief and over time is a clear negative signal.

bank.question: Which four-week practice plan is most likely to build lasting skill?
options: One long rehearsal the night before each important talk, with no breaks
Watching famous speakers without practising yourself
Short weekly talks, each with a goal, feedback and a note
Practising only when a big presentation is announced
bank.explanation: Regular, focused practice with feedback follows the plan, practise, record, feedback and adjust cycle, which builds skill over time.
